title: Imperative advice openers for communication/empathy
description: This latent fires on the sentence-initial words of imperative or prescriptive advice clauses, especially ones recommending communication-related behaviors ('By communicating...', 'Remember to...', 'Try to...', 'Be patient...', 'Consider...') as well as numbered list markers ('3.', '4.') that introduce such advice items. It activates most strongly on short fragments that begin an instruction/recommendation, particularly ones invoking empathy, openness, honesty, or prioritizing dialogue in interpersonal conflict, and also on bare list numbers that structurally cue an upcoming piece of advice. It does not activate on fully-formed descriptive or evaluative sentences that discuss feelings, situations, or judgments without an imperative/prescriptive framing (e.g., statements explaining why something is unfair, describing someone's emotional state, or offering an opinion on blame), even if they share the same topic of relationships or communication.

title: Verdict on someone's reaction as unacceptable
description: This latent fires on short, blunt evaluative statements in interpersonal-advice/AITA-style text that pass a strong moral verdict on a person's reaction or behavior, labeling it 'unacceptable,' 'unreasonable,' 'unfair,' or 'ridiculous' (e.g., 'Susan's reaction is completely unacceptable,' 'The mother's reaction was unfair and unreasonable'). It also fires heavily on bare numbered-list markers ('2.', '3.', '4.'), which in this corpus typically enumerate the supporting reasons or steps that follow such a verdict statement. It does not activate on the more hedged, advice-giving or empathetic sentences common elsewhere in the corpus (e.g., suggestions to communicate, set boundaries, or acknowledge mixed feelings), nor on neutral descriptive or narrative sentences that don't render a clear-cut condemnatory judgment.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral or bullet marker that begins an enumerated list item (e.g., '2', '3.', '4.', '9', '**') rather than on the content of the list item itself. The top-activating examples are almost purely the digit/marker token, often followed by a period or bold formatting, from advice-style numbered lists (e.g., step 1, step 2...). It also weakly activates on later list items embedded in fuller sentences (random examples), where a numbered/bulleted structure with bold headers ('**Keep an eye...**') is present. It would not activate on ordinary prose sentences lacking list formatting or explicit enumeration markers, even if they discuss similar advice-giving content.
